unit.title: Manage budgets and financial plans within the work team

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.topic: Linking finance to the team's plan
questions.stem: Nadine Clarke leads a team of eight in a Kingston insurance office. Her manager gives her a share of the department's budget for the year. What should she do first?
options: Spend the largest items early, before prices rise
Match the money to the team's work plan and see what it must cover
Ask each team member to choose one item to buy
Keep a quarter of it back in case the department cuts it later in the year

questions.topic: Linking finance to the team's plan
questions.stem: What is a team financial plan mainly meant to show?
options: The salary of each team member, for others to compare
The firm's profit for the year and the share price
What resources the team's work needs, what they cost and when
A list of everything the team has bought over the past five years

questions.stem: A hotel's housekeeping supervisor must plan next quarter's costs. Which information is most useful to start with?
options: The colours chosen for the new room curtains
The number of staff who took leave last year
The supervisor's own view of what feels about right
Expected room occupancy, staffing levels and supply usage rates

questions.stem: Four staff each work about 10 hours of overtime a month at J$1,200 an hour. What should the team's monthly overtime plan be?
A team plans a one-day client workshop: venue J$180,000, lunch for 60 people at J$2,500 each, and materials J$45,000. What is the total cost?
A team's J$2,400,000 budget is split 50% training, 30% equipment and 20% supplies. How much is allocated to equipment?
The team's requests add up to more than its budget. How should the team leader decide what to fund?
options: Fund the requests from the most senior members first
Cut every request by the same percentage without discussion
Fund the requests that were handed in earliest
Rank them by how much each helps the team meet its targets

questions.stem: Why should a team leader involve team members when drawing up the team's financial plan?
options: They know the real costs of the work and are more likely to support the plan
It allows the team leader to hand over all of her responsibility for the budget
The team members must legally sign every financial plan
It means the plan never needs to be checked by finance

questions.stem: Who else should a team leader usually consult before finalising the team's financial plan?
options: The firm's customers, by an online survey
Her manager and the finance staff who support the team
The team members' families, who are affected by overtime
No one else, as the team's plan is its own business

questions.stem: A team's plan depends on a large order from one client that may be delayed. What is the best way to prepare?
options: Ignore the risk, because the client has always paid in the past
Spend the whole budget early in the year so that it cannot be taken back
Plan what to cut or delay if the order slips, and agree it in advance
Ask the client to pay a large deposit before any talks begin

questions.stem: A team leader plans for a 'best case', 'expected case' and 'worst case' level of work. What is this technique called?
options: Zero-based costing
Benchmarking
Brainstorming
Scenario planning

questions.stem: A team leader is allowed to hold 5% of a J$3,000,000 team budget as a contingency. How much is that?
The team financial plan is approved. What is the best way to share it with the team?
options: Put it on the noticeboard and say nothing more about it to anyone
Brief the team on the plan, the limits and who looks after each part
Keep it private, as money matters are only for managers
Tell the team only when the money has run out

questions.stem: Why should each team member know which costs they are personally responsible for controlling?
options: So that they can be blamed for any overspend in the team
So that they can spend freely on their own areas without asking first
So that they can make sensible choices and spot problems early
So that the team leader need not check spending at all

questions.stem: A new team member at a Mandeville wholesaler does not know how to raise a purchase request. What should the team leader do?
options: Raise all his requests for him from now on
Let him learn by making his own mistakes for the first few weeks
Tell him to ask the supplier how to do it
Show him the procedure, the forms and who approves them

questions.stem: Team members often send incomplete expense claims, and finance sends them back. What is the most useful action for the team leader?
options: Hold a short session on the claim rules and give a checklist
Complain to finance that its rules are too strict for the team
Approve the claims anyway and let finance fix them
Stop all expense claims until the end of the quarter

questions.stem: A team member asks Garfield Thompson, his team leader, to approve a purchase that breaks the firm's buying procedure but 'will save time'. What should Garfield do?
options: Approve it this once, as the saving of time is worth it
Explain why the procedure matters and help him follow it
Approve it but ask him not to tell anyone in finance
Send the request back to him with no explanation of the reason

questions.stem: How often should a team leader review the team's spending against its financial plan?
options: Only at the end of the year, when the accounts are done
Only when finance raises a concern about the team
Regularly, such as monthly, using the finance report and the team's own records
Every hour, so that no purchase is made without the leader knowing

questions.stem: The team leader of a call centre in Portmore wants team members to see how the team is doing against its cost plan. What is the best method?
options: Email each member their own share of the team's costs privately each month
Wait until the yearly review to show the full figures
Show only the costs that are under the plan
Share a simple monthly chart at the team meeting and discuss it

questions.stem: Spending on printing is well above the team's plan for two months running. What should the team leader do first?
options: Find out with the team why printing has risen
Ban all printing in the team at once
Ask finance to move the printing cost to another team's budget
Wait to see whether it falls by itself

questions.stem: In one month the team spent J$1,350,000 and processed 4,500 applications. What was the cost per application?
Why is 'cost per item processed' a useful measure for a team, as well as the total spent?
options: It is the only figure that the auditors will ever ask to see
It makes the team's total spending look smaller than it is
It shows whether the team is using money efficiently as its workload changes
It removes the need for the team to keep any spending records of its own

questions.stem: Which approach to cutting team costs is most likely to work without harming service?
options: Cut the same amount from every line without looking at its purpose
Stop all staff training for the rest of the year
Delay paying suppliers so that the money stays in the bank
Ask the team for ideas and test each one against its effect on service

questions.stem: Moving team reports from paper to screens would save 12,000 pages a month at J$8 a page. What is the yearly saving?
A team member asks for a scanner costing J$240,000 that would save J$20,000 a month in courier and filing costs. How long would it take to pay for itself?
options: 6 months
12 months
20 months
24 months

questions.stem: When judging a team member's request for new equipment, which question matters most?
options: Is it the newest model on the market this year?
Has another team in the firm already bought the same kind of item?
Do the benefits to the team's work outweigh the full cost?
Will the team member be upset if the request is refused?

questions.stem: Halfway through the year, a team leader can see that a price rise will push the team over its plan. What should she do?
options: Say nothing for now and hope that enough savings appear later in the year
Hide the extra cost under a different heading
Stop all spending until the new year begins
Tell her manager early, with the figures and options to cover it

questions.stem: What should a team leader's note to her manager about a financial problem include?
options: The cause, the amount, the effect on the plan and her proposed action
Only the size of the overspend, rounded to the nearest million dollars
A list of the team members she blames for the problem
A request for more money with no reasons given

questions.stem: Why should a team keep its own simple record of what it has ordered and spent?
options: So that it never has to read the finance report
So that it can check the finance report and spot errors or missing items
So that it can spend more than the plan without finance noticing
So that each member can see the others' expense claims

questions.stem: A team's spending sheet is kept on one member's personal laptop. What is the main risk?
options: The sheet will use up too much storage space on the member's laptop
Other members may find it too easy to read
The record may be lost, changed or seen without control
Finance will want to see it more often than usual

questions.stem: A supplier offers the team leader a personal discount on a television if the team keeps buying its stationery. What should she do?
options: Accept, as the discount is for her and not the firm
Accept, but share the discount with the team
Accept only if the stationery price stays the same
Refuse and report the offer under the firm's rules

questions.stem: A team member is found to have claimed taxi fares for trips she did not make. What should the team leader do?
options: Report it and follow the firm's procedure, keeping the facts confidential
Deal with it quietly by asking her to buy lunch for the team
Tell the rest of the team at the next meeting as a warning
Ignore it, as the amounts were small

questions.topic: Involving the team in cost control
questions.stem: What most helps team members feel responsible for the team's costs?
options: Being told by the team leader that the budget is 'not their concern'
Understanding the plan and seeing how their choices affect it
Being fined for every small overspend
Having all spending decisions taken away from them

questions.topic: Involving the team in cost control
questions.stem: A team of school office staff suggests a way to cut photocopier costs. The idea works. What should the team leader do?
options: Take the credit for it herself when reporting the saving to the principal
Say nothing, as staff are paid to think of savings
Thank the team, report the saving and say who suggested it
Use the saving to buy items for her own office

questions.stem: The firm adds a new service, and the team's workload will rise by a third from next quarter. What should happen to the team's financial plan?
options: Nothing, as the plan was approved at the start of the year
The team should absorb the extra work within the old figures
The team leader should spend extra money and explain later
It should be revised and the change agreed with her manager

questions.stem: The team will be under its plan at year end because a post was vacant for four months. What should the team leader do with this?
options: Report it early, so that the money can be used well elsewhere
Spend it quickly on items the team does not need, before the year ends
Hide it so that next year's plan is not reduced
Use it to pay the team a bonus without approval

questions.stem: Three staff each work an extra 8 hours on a Saturday at J$1,500 an hour. What is the cost of the Saturday?
Overtime in the team keeps rising because work arrives unevenly through the week. Which action is most likely to cut the cost?
options: Pay every member a fixed amount of overtime each week, whatever the work
Ban overtime and let work wait until it is done
Plan rosters around the busy days the records show
Hire two new full-time staff straight away

questions.stem: At year end, a team leader wants to judge how well the team managed its money. Which question is most useful?
options: Did the team spend every dollar of the budget it was given?
Did any team member ever question the financial plan?
Was the team's spending the lowest in the whole firm?
Did the team meet its targets within the plan, and were forecasts accurate?

questions.stem: A review finds the team's plan was always wrong on supplies because usage was guessed. What should the team leader recommend?
options: Base next year's figures on recorded usage rates and expected workload
Leave the supplies line out of next year's plan altogether and see what happens
Add a large extra amount to supplies to be safe
Ask the supplier how much the team should plan to buy

questions.stem: Why should a team leader write down what worked and what did not in managing the team's money this year?
options: Because the auditors require a written diary from every team in the firm
So that next year's plan and procedures can be improved
So that blame can be placed on the right person
Because finance cannot produce reports without it

questions.stem: A team leader keeps a spreadsheet of planned and actual costs by month. Which feature makes it most useful?
options: Bright colours in every cell
A different layout every month
Formulas that show the difference and the total to date
Figures typed in as text so they cannot change

questions.stem: Two suppliers quote for team training. One is J$90,000 cheaper, but its trainers have no experience in the subject. What should the team leader weigh?
options: Only the price, as savings are always the main goal
Only the supplier the team used last time
Only which supplier can start the soonest
Price against quality and the results the training must achieve

questions.topic: Linking finance to the team's plan
questions.stem: A team leader's financial plan and the team's work plan were written separately and do not match. What problem is most likely?
options: Money is planned for the wrong things or at the wrong times
The team will have too much work to do and not enough staff to do it
The finance system will refuse to accept the plan
The team will have to be closed by the end of the year

questions.stem: A team in a public agency finds it can save money by buying from a single supplier it likes, without quotes. What should guide the decision?
options: The team leader's personal trust in that supplier
The public procurement rules and value for money
What the team did at a previous employer
Whichever choice is quickest for the team

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What two-word term names planning for best, expected and worst cases of workload or cost?
What two-word term names the comparison of what a proposal will cost with what it will gain?
What is the time it takes for savings to repay the cost of a purchase called? (Two words, or one with 'period'.)
Lunch is needed for 45 people at J$2,200 each. What is the catering cost, in J$?
A team spent J$840,000 handling 3,500 orders. What was the cost per order, in J$?
A team budget of J$1,800,000 gives 25% to training. How much is that, in J$?
A machine costs J$300,000 and saves J$25,000 a month. How many months does it take to pay for itself?
What one-word term names a small sum held back in a plan to meet costs that cannot be foreseen?
What two-word term names the value of the next best use given up when the team spends money one way rather than another?
Five staff each work 6 hours of overtime at J$1,400 an hour. What is the overtime cost, in J$?
What three-letter term names a measure, such as cost per order, used to track how well a team is doing against its goals?
A change saves the team J$15,000 a month from month 4 to month 12 of its year. What is the total saving for the year, in J$?

shortAnswers.topic: Linking finance to the team's plan
shortAnswers.stem: What two-word term names the unit of an organisation, such as a team or department, to which costs are charged and for which a manager is answerable?
A team holds 4% of its J$2,500,000 budget as a contingency. How much is held, in J$?
In a spreadsheet, what is the instruction called that works out a value automatically, such as the difference between plan and actual?

essays.stem: You lead a team of ten in a regional office. Describe how you would prepare the team's financial plan for the coming year, working from the team's work plan.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start from the team's work plan and targets for the year, because the money should follow the work. For each activity I would list the resources it needs: staff time and overtime, equipment, supplies, training, travel and services. I would use records of past usage and expected workload to estimate quantities, and current prices or quotes to cost them, writing down each assumption. I would ask team members who run each activity to check the estimates, since they know the real costs. I would then phase the costs by month to match when the work happens, and compare the total with the amount the department has given us. If the requests are too high, I would rank them by how much they help the team meet its targets and agree changes with my manager. I would include a small contingency and a plan for what to cut if work or prices change. Finally I would confirm the plan with finance and my manager before briefing the team.
markingPoints: Starts from the team's work plan and targets
Identifies and costs the resources each activity needs, with assumptions
Involves team members and uses records of past usage
Phases costs, compares with the allocation and prioritises if short
Includes contingency and confirms the plan with manager and finance

essays.stem: Evaluate the benefits and drawbacks of involving team members in planning and managing the team's money, and recommend how far a team leader should involve them.
essays.modelAnswer: Involving the team brings better information, because members know how much stock, overtime and travel the work really needs. It builds ownership, so members are more careful with spending they helped plan, and it develops their skills for future roles. It also brings cost-saving ideas from the people who do the work. The drawbacks are that it takes time, some members may ask for more than they need to protect their own area, and not everyone has the skills to estimate costs. Some figures, such as individual pay, are confidential and cannot be shared. Final responsibility stays with the team leader, so involvement must not blur who is accountable. I recommend involving members in estimating the costs of the activities they run, in suggesting savings and in reviewing monthly results at team meetings, while the team leader sets priorities, checks the estimates, keeps confidential items private and makes the final decisions with her manager.
markingPoints: Benefits: better information, ownership and ideas
Benefits: develops members' skills
Drawbacks: time, inflated requests, skills gaps, confidentiality
Notes that accountability stays with the team leader
Makes a clear recommendation on what to involve members in

essays.stem: Your team will run a one-day client workshop: venue J$180,000, lunch for 60 people at J$2,500 each, and materials J$45,000. Your allocation for the event is J$400,000. Work out the cost, judge the plan and say how you would manage the risk of more people attending.
essays.modelAnswer: Lunch costs 60 × J$2,500 = J$150,000. The total is J$180,000 + J$150,000 + J$45,000 = J$375,000. This is J$25,000 below the J$400,000 allocation, which leaves a small margin of about 6% for changes. The main risk is that more clients attend. Each extra guest adds J$2,500 for lunch and some materials, so ten more guests would add at least J$25,000, using up the whole margin. To manage this I would ask clients to register by a fixed date and confirm final numbers with the caterer a few days before, choosing a caterer whose price is per head. I would set a maximum number to match the venue and budget. I would check whether the venue price includes equipment, to avoid hidden costs, and get written quotes. If numbers rose above the limit, I would agree options with my manager in advance, such as a cheaper lunch or printing materials in smaller numbers. After the event I would record the actual cost against the plan.
markingPoints: Lunch J$150,000 and total J$375,000 correct
Compares with the J$400,000 allocation (J$25,000 margin)
Works out the effect of extra guests (J$2,500 each)
Controls numbers: registration deadline, maximum, per-head pricing, written quotes
Agrees fallback options in advance and records actual against plan

essays.stem: Describe how you would brief your team on its approved financial plan, and explain what each member needs to understand.
essays.modelAnswer: I would hold a team meeting soon after approval, with a one-page summary and a simple chart rather than the full spreadsheet. I would explain how the plan links to our targets, so members see that the money supports the work. I would show the main headings, such as overtime, supplies, training and travel, and the amount for each. I would make clear who is responsible for which costs, for example the stores clerk for supplies and the shift leads for overtime, and what each person may spend or must ask about first. I would remind everyone of the firm's financial procedures for purchase requests and expense claims, and where to find the forms. I would explain how we will track spending, with a monthly chart at team meetings, and that problems should be raised early rather than hidden. I would invite questions and ideas for saving money. Confidential items such as individual pay would not be shown. Finally, I would send the summary and procedures to everyone after the meeting.
markingPoints: Uses a meeting with a clear summary, linked to team targets
Explains the main headings and amounts
Makes each member's responsibilities and limits clear
Reminds of procedures and how spending will be tracked and problems raised
Invites questions and ideas, keeps confidential items private, and follows up in writing

essays.stem: Explain how a team leader can support team members to follow the organisation's financial procedures, and why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Procedures for buying, claiming expenses and handling cash protect the firm's money, keep records accurate for audit and tax, and prevent fraud and waste. They only work if staff follow them. A team leader supports this first by making sure everyone knows the procedures: an induction for new members, a short refresher when rules change, and quick guides or checklists for common tasks such as purchase requests. She should explain why each step exists, because people follow rules they understand. She should be easy to ask, answer questions quickly and check the first few forms a new member completes. She must follow the procedures herself and never ask staff to bypass them. When errors happen, she should coach rather than blame, and look for causes, such as a confusing form, that she can raise with finance. Repeated or deliberate breaches must be reported and dealt with under the firm's rules. Good support means fewer rejected forms, faster payments and less risk.
markingPoints: Explains why procedures matter (protecting money, records, fraud prevention)
Ensures members know the procedures through induction, refreshers and guides
Explains reasons and is available to answer and check work
Leads by example and coaches on errors, raising unclear steps with finance
Reports deliberate or repeated breaches under the firm's rules

essays.stem: Plan a simple system for monitoring your team's spending against its financial plan during the year.
essays.modelAnswer: I would set up a shared spreadsheet, kept in a controlled folder, with the plan for each heading by month and columns for actual spending, the difference and the total to date, using formulas. Team members responsible for each heading would log orders and claims as they happen, so that we know about costs before finance's report arrives. Each month I would compare our records with finance's report and sort out any differences. I would track one or two measures that link money to work, such as cost per application and overtime hours per week, so that we can see whether spending makes sense as workload changes. At the monthly team meeting I would show a simple chart and ask the people responsible to explain big differences. I would agree in advance what counts as a difference worth acting on. Anything that threatens the plan would go to my manager early, with options. At the end of each quarter I would update the forecast for the rest of the year.
markingPoints: A controlled record of plan, actual and differences by month
Members log their own spending as it happens
Monthly comparison with finance's report
Measures that link spending to workload
Team review, agreed action level, early reporting and quarterly update

essays.stem: Your manager asks your team to cut its costs by 8% for the rest of the year without harming service. Plan how you would do this with your team.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first explain the reason and the target to the team, so that they understand the pressure and do not fear for their jobs without cause. I would then review our spending with them, heading by heading, to see which costs are essential to service and which are not. I would hold a short ideas session, asking each member for ways to save, such as reducing printing, sharing deliveries, planning rosters around busy days to cut overtime and delaying non-urgent purchases. For each idea we would estimate the saving and check its effect on service, safety and staff wellbeing. I would choose the set that reaches the 8% with the least harm, give each action an owner and a date, and agree the plan with my manager. I would avoid cutting training or maintenance that would cost more later. Each month we would track the savings against the target at team meetings, recognise good ideas, and adjust if any action hurt service.
markingPoints: Explains the reason and target to the team
Reviews spending to separate essential from non-essential costs
Gathers ideas from the team and estimates each saving and its effect on service
Agrees a plan with owners, dates and manager approval, avoiding false savings
Tracks savings, recognises ideas and adjusts

essays.stem: A team member asks for a J$240,000 scanner that would save J$20,000 a month in courier and filing costs. Evaluate the request and recommend a decision.
essays.modelAnswer: The payback period is J$240,000 ÷ J$20,000 = 12 months, so the scanner would repay its cost in one year, and over three years it would save J$720,000 against its cost of J$240,000, a net gain of J$480,000 before running costs. That is a strong case if the figures are sound. I would check the saving estimate: how many courier trips and filing hours it replaces, and whether those costs will really stop. I would add running costs such as maintenance, software and staff training, which reduce the saving. I would ask about other benefits, such as faster service and less lost paper, and risks, such as the need to store scanned files securely under the data protection law. I would also check whether the team's plan has room for the cost this year, or whether it needs approval from my manager, and get at least two quotes. If the checks support the figures, I recommend buying the scanner, and tracking the saving after six months.
markingPoints: Payback 12 months correct, and longer-term saving considered
Tests the saving estimate and adds running costs
Considers other benefits and risks, including data security
Checks budget room, approval and quotes
Makes a clear recommendation with a follow-up check

essays.stem: In month seven, you see that a supplier price rise will put your team about J$200,000 over its plan by year end. Explain what you would do and how you would report it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first check the figures: the new prices, how much we still need to buy and when, so that the J$200,000 estimate is sound. Then I would look for ways to cover it within the team: other suppliers or products of the same quality, buying less where we can, and savings on other headings such as printing or travel. I would talk to the team members who manage supplies, as they may know options I do not. I would then report to my manager without delay, because early warning gives more choices. My note would state the cause, the amount and timing, the effect on the team's plan, the savings we can make ourselves, and what is still left over, with options such as moving money from another heading with approval, or delaying a planned purchase. I would ask for a decision by a set date. Afterwards I would update the plan, tell the team what has changed, and use the lesson to set better price assumptions next year.
markingPoints: Checks the size and timing of the problem
Looks for ways to cover it within the team, involving members
Reports early to the manager
Report gives cause, amount, effect, own savings and options
Updates the plan, tells the team and records the lesson

essays.stem: At the end of the year, how would you evaluate how well your team managed its budget and financial plan? Recommend how the findings should be used.
essays.modelAnswer: I would compare the final spending with the plan for each heading and find the reasons for the big differences, separating changes in workload from changes in price or efficiency. I would look at whether the team met its targets with the money, using measures such as cost per item processed. I would judge the planning: were our estimates and assumptions accurate, and was the contingency right? I would judge the process: did team members follow procedures, were forms rejected, were records accurate and did they agree with finance's reports, and were problems raised early? I would ask the team in a short review meeting what helped and what got in the way. I would write a brief report to my manager with the results, the lessons and recommendations, for example basing supplies on recorded usage, training a member in purchase requests, or changing the monthly review. The findings should be used to build next year's plan, improve procedures and develop team members' financial skills.
markingPoints: Compares actual with plan and explains the main differences
Judges results against targets and efficiency measures
Evaluates the accuracy of estimates and the working of procedures and records
Involves the team in the review and reports to the manager
Uses findings to improve next year's plan, procedures and skills

practical1.title: Prepare and brief a team financial plan for the next quarter
practical1.brief: Your group is the leadership of a customer service team in a firm with offices in Kingston and Ocho Rios. The assessor gives you the team's work plan for next quarter (targets, staff, planned activities and a client event) and a price list, plus the amount the department has allocated. Prepare the team's financial plan for the quarter. Give each member a named role: team leader (sets priorities and checks the whole plan), staff costs planner (staff time and overtime), activities costing officer (supplies, equipment, training and the client event), contingency and risk officer (scenarios and what to cut if work or prices change), and in a group of five a communications officer (prepares the one-page summary and the responsibilities chart). Produce: (1) a costed plan by month in a spreadsheet or on paper, compared with the allocation; (2) a contingency plan for one risk; (3) a chart showing which team member looks after which costs; and (4) a 10-minute team briefing, role-played with the assessor as a team member. Every member speaks in the briefing.
materials: Assessor's pack: work plan, price list and allocation
Computer with spreadsheet and printer, or squared paper and calculators
photos: The planning flipchart with each member's name and role
The costed plan by month, with the total compared with the allocation
The contingency plan for the chosen risk
The team briefing in progress with the one-page summary
checklist: Carried out a named role and produced their own part of the evidence
Costs are linked to the activities in the work plan and worked out correctly
Plan is compared with the allocation and priorities are set if it is short
Contingency plan names a real risk, its cost effect and agreed actions
Responsibilities chart gives each cost heading an owner
Spoke clearly in the briefing and explained their part of the plan
Answered the assessor's questions about the figures
safety: Use made-up names and figures; no real staff pay details
Keep spreadsheets in the Centre's shared folder and delete copies from personal devices
Respect each member's views and share the workload fairly
Take a short screen break each hour

practical2.title: Run a team cost-saving workshop and review the team's financial processes
practical2.brief: Your group is a team in a hotel's administration office. The assessor gives you six months of the team's planned and actual costs, a list of three problems (for example, rejected expense claims, rising overtime and a printing overspend) and the team's financial procedures. First, read the figures and agree where the team is off its plan. Then run a 30-minute cost-saving workshop: gather ideas, estimate the saving from each, check its effect on guest service and staff wellbeing, and choose the best set. Finally, write a one-page review of how the team manages its money (planning, procedures, records and reporting) with recommendations for improvement, addressed to the office manager. Give each member a named role: facilitator (runs the workshop), analyst (works out the savings), recorder (keeps the ideas sheet and action list), report writer, and in a group of five a reviewer who checks the team's procedures against the problems. Every member must contribute ideas in the workshop. Photograph each stage.
materials: Assessor's pack: six months of figures, problem list and procedures
Ideas sheet and action list templates
Paper or a computer for the report

checklist: Carried out a named role and contributed to the evidence
Read the figures correctly and identified the main problems
Offered at least one practical saving idea in the workshop
Savings are estimated correctly and checked against effects on service and staff
Action list gives each chosen idea an owner and a date
Review identifies weaknesses in planning, procedures or records with clear recommendations
Treated other members' ideas with respect
safety: Keep the figures confidential and collect all copies at the end
Discuss processes and costs, not named individuals
Check that no saving idea harms safety or staff wellbeing
Share tasks fairly so that no member is overloaded
